HEADER:
Date: 2026-07-21 | 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Meeting ID: ff-2026-07-21-archipelago-001
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jon (Redwood SE), Ethan (Archipelago Head of ML), Priya (Infra), Marco (PM)

AUTO SUMMARY (auto-generated):
- Quick intake on cost per token and options to lower unit economics via batching, caching, and quantized model variants.
- Security requirements flagged for Private/VPC option (KMS, audit logs, SSO).

---- TRANSCRIPT ----
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're excited to dig into the unit econ stuff, i think jon and i will start with a quick set of questions about your workload and then jump into tradeoffs, sound good?
[00:06] Ethan: yeah that works, thanks maya, i'll just say up front cost is like the gating factor for us, we have to bring per-interaction to under $0.002 ideally.
[00:14] Jon: ok, could you give us the typical request shape? tokens in, tokens out, are these short scoring calls or long generation?
[00:21] Marco: mostly short scoring, 8-24 token completions for snippets, plus embeddings for similarity, so two different bill lines basically, and some reranking where we do maybe 1-2 prefix tokens repeated a lot.
[00:34] Priya: also note traffic is bursty — market open spikes, maybe 3-5x baseline for 20-30 minutes, then drops.
[00:40] Jon: got it. For short completions we usually talk about batching windows — if you're willing to accept p95 of ~200-300ms we can batch a bit to improve tokens/sec. If you need sub-100ms p95 we push towards single-request low-latency paths or dedicated smaller batch sizes.
[00:55] Ethan: and how does that map to cost? like if we go from 100ms to 300ms, what's the delta on per-token?
[01:02] Maya: ballpark: higher batching improves GPU utilization — you can see 2-4x cost reduction on token compute depending on model and quantization. but there's also prefix caching, which for your reranking/prefix-mostly workload could cut repeated context cost dramatically.
[01:18] Marco: prefix caching? can you walk through an example?
[01:22] Jon: sure — imagine you have a 50-token prefix that's the same across many requests, we can cache the KV cache so the model doesn't recompute those tokens every time. In practice that means subsequent requests only pay for the delta tokens. For your use case where a 2-token user-specific prompt is appended to a stable prefix, that's huge.
[01:40] Priya: does that work across hosted and dedicated? any data residency problems?
[01:44] Jon: yes — caching is implemented in the runtime and works in both hosted and dedicated modes. For private deployments, caching runs inside your VPC so data never leaves the network. We'll note compliance constraints though — caches are ephemeral and we can tie TTLs and auditing to them.
[01:58] Ethan: you mentioned quantized models — we worry about quality drop. what are the options?
[02:03] Jon: today we support int8 and 4-bit quantized variants for a lot of open models. For short completions often the quality delta is small; for very sensitive outputs we'd recommend A/B against your evaluation set. We can run a quality-preserving quant profile and present tradeoffs.
[02:17] Marco: and switching model variants — hosted supports fallbacks, right? like if quantized path is missing capacity?
[02:22] Maya: yes, smart routing can fallback to a compatible variant (higher precision or different instance) but those fallbacks can increase unit cost and latency — we surface that in the console.
[02:34] Ethan: what's the rough pricing differences between hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved?
[02:38] Maya: Hosted is pay-as-you-go — per-token compute + infra margin. Dedicated is a reserved capacity model — you commit to GPUs for a period and get a much lower effective per-token if your utilization is high. For bursty patterns the key is burst capacity and autoscaling in Dedicated or hybrid routing where burst goes to hosted.
[02:55] Priya: can you do hybrid? route normal traffic to dedicated and overflow to hosted?
[02:59] Jon: absolutely — that's a common pattern. You configure routing policies by latency tier or cost tier; Redwood will automatically route overflow to hosted variants if dedicated capacity is saturated.
[03:09] Ethan: latency SLOs with bursts — how predictable is p95 when you have overflow to hosted?
[03:13] Jon: it depends on model and region; in practice we see a small bump on p95 during overflow but the routing policy can prioritize latency-sensitive requests to remain on dedicated while lower-priority requests overflow. We can also set hard caps to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[03:25] Marco: ok, hypothetically if we want to target $0.0015 per interaction on average, with 3k daily qps and 3x burst, what should we be thinking?
[03:33] Maya: quick gut — you'd likely need a dedicated commit sized to cover baseline, use prefix caching for repeated context, and quantized variants for lower-cost bulk scoring. We'll need exact prompt sizes and token counts to model.
[03:44] Ethan: we'll share traces.
[03:46] Priya: security — we require SSO, SAML, KMS integration and audit logs for all production deployments. SOC2 is a must. Do you support customer-managed keys?
[03:56] Jon: yes, Private supports KMS/HSM integration and Dedicated can be configured with customer-managed key options; audit logs and retention policies are configurable. We'll include SOC2 docs in the packet.
[04:07] Ethan: for Private/on-prem, what's the difference in unit cost? it seems like more overhead but maybe cheaper per token long-run?
[04:13] Maya: Private has higher upfront engineering/ops cost but you get control over hardware and sometimes lower margins vs hosted. Per-token compute depends on the hardware you provide and utilization; if you can run large-volume steady-state it can be lowest cost. For Archipelago's bursty pattern maybe Dedicated + hosted overflow is simpler.
[04:29] Marco: how do you handle KV cache eviction and consistency? if we have segmented prefixes per customer, are they isolated?
[04:36] Jon: KV cache is namespace-isolated per customer and can be sharded by tenant. Eviction is LRU with TTLs and we expose metrics for cache hit rate. For strict consistency there's options to pin entries for short durations; would need to discuss specifics.
[04:48] Ethan: any gotchas with embeddings — pricing and batching differ, right?
[04:51] Jon: yes, embeddings are billed differently (vector units) and you can batch embeddings at higher throughput since compute per vector is lower, but GPU memory and IO are considerations. We can show a model where embeddings are computed in dedicated pools optimized for throughput and completions in low-latency pools.
[05:05] Priya: about benchmarking — can you replicate our burst profile, meaning the 3-5x spikes?
[05:09] Jon: we can run stress tests that mimic your burst windows and show latency and unit cost across percentiles. We'll also try caching and batching knobs to show marginal gains.
[05:17] Marco: what's required from us to start a pilot?
[05:20] Maya: sample traces, evaluation prompt sets, success metric (cost per interaction target + p95 target), and an internal sponsor for procurement. We'll map you to a pilot agreement with a small reserved capacity and a short trial.
[05:32] Ethan: procurement — any standard contract length for Dedicated?
[05:35] Maya: typical is 6-12 months for committed Dedicated, shorter pilots can be month-to-month for reserved dev pools. We'll surface flexible commit options.
[05:44] Marco: competitors — are there things we should watch out for?
[05:47] Jon: some providers are simpler but opaque on performance; others have lower sticker price but limited control over routing and cache. We'll share a competitive note.
[05:56] Maya: ok i'm going to recap next steps: jon will run a benchmark if you share traces; i'll send pricing and SOC2/kms docs; ethan will confirm timeline for pilot decision. Anything to add?
[06:06] Ethan: no that's it, thanks.
[06:09] Maya: great, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark slot. thanks everyone.
